parts:
There might be other issues I haven't noticed, but here's what jumps out immediately:

1) You can't do this

l[1] <- y[1];
b[1] <-0;

in the transformed parameters block or in the model block because you're trying to assign real values to what you've declared to be unknown values (i.e. parameters). l[1] and b[1] should be declared in transformed data block (since you're assigning them values) and then you can define l_temp and b_temp in transformed parameters to be n-1 vectors of parameters instead of n vectors. Then l and b can be defined as local variables in the model block and constructed from l_1 and l_temp, and b_1 and b_temp, respectively.  

transformed data {
 real l_1 ;
 real b_1 ;

 l_1 <- y[1] ;
 b_1 <- 0 ;
}
transformed parameters{
 vector<lower=0> [n-1] l_temp ;
 vector[n-1] b_temp ;
}
model{
 vector[n] l ;
 vector[n] b ;
 l[1] <- l_1 ;
 b[1] <- b_1 ;
 for (i in 2:n) {
  l[i] <- l_temp[i] ;
  b[i] <- b_temp[i] ;
 }
}

And then you can use l and b in the rest of the model block. 

There's a similar problem with positiveInnovations and negativeInnovations.

2) In the first model you declare trendError and levelError to be transformed parameters but they should just be parameters. 

3) In the second model you try using sampling statements with variables declared in the model block, but these need to be parameters (or transformed parameters if appropriate). 


Maybe try fixing those things and see if you still get errors.

messages.subject: Re: trying to fit a state-space model
parts:
I don't know enough about these models to speak to the statistics behind it, but a few things seem a bit strange :

- You've declared your data y to be positive but you're using the student_t distribution which has support on the negative reals too. 
- Why does sigma have to be greater than 0.05? Unless that's some peculiarity about these models, you're probably better of without the truncation. Maybe try a prior that doesn't have a lot of mass right near 0 but don't use the hard constraint unless you have to for some reason. Furthermore, MIN_SIGMA doesn't have the same value as the lower bound on sigma when it's declared as a parameter. If you absolutely need to truncate sigma slightly above zero then you should declare that value as the lower bound in the parameters block rather than 0.  

Hopefully somebody else who is more familiar with these models will have some other and better suggestions.

tail(y,n-1) ~ student_t(nu, head(l,n-1) + head(b,n-1), sigma);

Be careful! using absolute values is very dangerous
as it will typically lead to two posterior modes depending
on how l and b are constrained. In your case, swapping
signs on l and b will lead to the same answer once you
apply fabs().


This could very likely be the cause of poor n_eff --- if
two chains land in different modes, R-hat and n_eff get very low because
they estimate means from all of the chains combined and
then make sure each chain matches the global mean.

The standard GLM solution if you want to constrain
a linear predictor to be positive is to exponentiate.

- Bob

On closer inspection I see you're using (lev - b) as
both a location and a scale adjustment, which should
identify your model.

Ideally you'd want to make sure that (lev - b) is positive
by some other means than fabs() just to ensure that the
model has support on all values of the parameters that
match the declared constraints.

But if you don't it's probably not a big deal in this model.

- Bob
